solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Edge has broken some pieces of glass instrument

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it, so 'Edge' goes into 'some pieces of glass'

parts.note: panes are sheets of glass in a window
to pip is to edge out, beat by a whisker

explanation.surface: Someone's nerves have given out and they have smashed a glass instrument such as a harmonica or pipette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edge' looks like a noun for a rim; it is the verb, as when a runner is pipped at the post. PANPIPES is PANES with PIP breaking in.
explanation.definitionFit: Panpipes are a wind instrument made of several tubes of graded length bound together, played by blowing across the tops.

clue.text: Courts offering protection to American country

indicators.note: a shield around something protects it, so 'Courts' wrap round 'American'

parts.note: atria are open inner courtyards, as in a Roman house
US is the standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Law courts are granting protection to an American citizen, perhaps in an asylum case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courts' suggests judges and law; here it is the plural of atrium, the open courtyard at the heart of a Roman house.
explanation.definitionFit: Austria is a nation in central Europe, a plain example of the category named.

clue.text: As are mum and dad, running this way and that?

definitions.text: As are mum and dad, running this way and that?

parts.words: mum and dad, running this way and that
parts.note: surface reading: two parents dashing about, busy with the household
setter's reading: the words 'mum' and 'dad' read the same forwards as backwards

explanation.walkthrough: The picture is harried parents; the trick is to look at the words themselves, which run the same either way. That property names the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes any word or phrase whose letters read identically in both directions, like mum, dad, level.

clue.text: Smoother, fifth design?

parts.note: a plan is a design or drawing
E is the fifth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: An art tutor muses on which of five designs is the most polished.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads in reverse of its printed order: the design comes first and the fifth letter tacks on after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter's plane is a tool pushed along wood to shave it flat, so it is literally something that makes surfaces even.

clue.text: Ungodly imbibing last of drink — isn't that enough?

indicators.note: to imbibe is to take in, so 'Ungodly' swallows the chosen letter

parts.note: sinful = wicked, godless

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, taken from 'drink'

parts.note: final letter of drink

explanation.surface: A disapproving onlooker watches a heathen drinker down one more and wonders whether they have had enough.
explanation.walkthrough: The drinking theme runs right through the surface, so the whole clue also points at the answer. SKINFUL is SINFUL taking in K.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinful is the amount of alcohol it takes to get thoroughly drunk; the question 'isn't that enough?' hints at it.

clue.text: Sweating perhaps, potting a red

indicators.note: potting puts a ball into a pocket, so 'a' is put inside 'Sweating perhaps'

parts.note: sweating skin is damp; 'perhaps' marks an example
the article as printed

explanation.surface: A snooker player is sweating under the lights while potting a red ball.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker the reds are the fifteen red balls; here 'red' is a communist, and the snooker verb 'potting' puts the article inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A Maoist follows the communist doctrine of Mao Zedong, and red is the usual shorthand for any communist.

clue.text: Vessel in my hands on film

parts.note: what is in my hands belongs to me: it is mine
a film is a thin layer, as of oil on water

explanation.surface: Someone holds a vessel, perhaps a cup, in their hands in a movie scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' wants to be a movie; it is a thin coating. In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A minelayer is a naval ship built to lay explosive mines at sea, so it is a kind of vessel.

clue.text: Long pole, gilded article?

indicators.note: gilding coats an object in gold, so gold is laid around 'article'

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A tall gilded pole is being offered as some item for sale or display.
explanation.walkthrough: Or is the heraldic word for gold, a crossword staple; wrapping the article in it gives OAR.
explanation.definitionFit: An oar is a lengthy shaft with a flat blade, used for rowing a boat.

clue.text: Launch escapade in flier

parts.note: to sky a ball is to hit or launch it high
a lark is a prank or escapade

explanation.surface: Someone sets off on a daring adventure in an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot or a plane; here it is a bird. The verb sky comes from cricket, where a batsman skies a ball straight up.
explanation.definitionFit: The skylark is a songbird famous for singing while it rises high into the air.

clue.text: A moralist with navy pants in charitable organisation

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are in a poor, jumbled state

parts.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters; 'with' joins the two parts

explanation.surface: A prim moralist wears navy trousers while working at a charity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' reads as trousers; it is the British slang verdict 'rubbish', telling you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The Salvation Army is a Christian church and worldwide relief body known for shelters and brass bands.

clue.text: French figure behind British sculpture

indicators.note: one thing behind another comes after it, so 'French figure' follows 'British'

parts.note: Br is a standard abbreviation of British
onze is French for eleven

explanation.surface: A French statue stands behind a British one in a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' reads as a statue, fitting the gallery; it is a number, and French makes it onze.
explanation.definitionFit: A bronze is a statue cast in that copper alloy, so the metal's name stands for the artwork.

clue.text: Misfire in defeat, accidental

parts.note: a fall is a defeat or downfall, as of a city
in music an accidental is a sign such as a flat or sharp

explanation.surface: A gun going off by mistake in a lost battle was purely accidental.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accidental' looks like an adjective; it is the musical noun for a sign that alters a note, of which a flat is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A joke or plan that falls flat fails to have its intended effect, which is what misfiring means figuratively.

clue.text: It's strong material that has my support in Scottish town

parts.note: to be for something is to back it
twill is a hard-wearing woven cloth
the supporter speaking: the phrase ends with the first person

explanation.surface: Someone vouches for a sturdy fabric made in a Highland town.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as a poetic sentence, 'For twill I am': twill has my support. That is what 'It's strong material that has my support' spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: Fort William is a town in the western Highlands of Scotland at the foot of Ben Nevis.

clue.text: Fresh sandwiches are prepared with first of processed cheese

indicators.note: a sandwich holds its filling inside, so 'Fresh' goes round the rest

parts.note: fresh weather is cool, chilly

indicators.note: prepared food has been worked on, so 'are' with that letter gets reworked

parts.note: anagram fodder, as printed

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, taken from 'processed'

parts.note: opening letter of processed

explanation.surface: A deli worker prepares fresh sandwiches and adds a slice of processed cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' looks like a description of the sandwiches; it is the cool weather sense, and 'sandwiches' is the verb doing the wrapping.
explanation.definitionFit: Caerphilly is a crumbly white Welsh variety named after the town where it was first made.

clue.text: Musical, musical bunch!

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
a spray is a small bunch of flowers

explanation.surface: An excited cry about a group of singers from a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'musical' is the show Hair, not an adjective describing the bunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairspray is a stage show, filmed too, set in 1960s Baltimore, about a teenager on a TV dance programme.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink for a king's nicked

indicators.note: nicked means stolen, so the letters are lifted from inside 'for a king's'

parts.note: the letters run across the end of 'for', all of 'a' and the start of 'king'

explanation.surface: Someone has stolen the king's liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a royal theft; 'nicked' is British slang for stolen, telling you letters are taken from the words beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Raki is an aniseed-flavoured spirit drunk in Turkey and the Balkans.

clue.text: Flower on end of tennis racket

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing on another follows it, so 'Flower' comes after
the end of a word is its last letter, taken from 'tennis'

parts.note: final letter of tennis
a flower is something that flows, a river: the Cam runs through Cambridge

explanation.surface: A flower has been tied to the end of a tennis racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; it is a river, the Cam, and 'racket' is not the tennis kind but a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a dishonest scheme to cheat people, and a scam is exactly such a fraud.

clue.text: Happy golfer just off the green?

definitions.meaning: first sense: an informal adjective for cheerful, lively
second sense: a golfer lying just off the green plays a short lofted chip shot, so is one who chips

explanation.surface: A golfer is pleased to have landed the ball just short of the green.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is invented for the joke: one who chips; the question mark flags the liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Chipper is an informal adjective for cheerful and bright, a straightforward synonym for happy.

clue.text: Twist that's baffling written in English

indicators.note: something baffling is confused, so 'written in' and the language letter are confused

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A plot twist in a novel written in English leaves readers baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Written in English' reads as a single phrase about language; only 'written in' is fodder, with English adding one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To intertwine things is to twist them together, as vines or threads wind round each other.

clue.text: Clear, after ascent, exercise unfinished — bit of a climber?

indicators.note: unfinished means lacking its end, so 'exercise' loses its last letter
in a down clue an ascent reads bottom to top, so 'Clear' is turned upside down

parts.note: net = clear, as in profit after deductions
drill, a training exercise, cut short

explanation.surface: A mountaineer clears a peak after an ascent, not finishing the exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' is not a mountaineer but a climbing plant, and the question mark signals the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A tendril is the slender coiling shoot by which a vine or pea grips a support, part of a climbing plant.

clue.text: Figure serving up seasonal drink soon

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means read bottom to top, so the drink and 'soon' are turned over

parts.note: nog, as in eggnog, is drunk at Christmas
anon is an old word for soon

explanation.surface: A host says they will be serving the Christmas punch soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' could be a number or a person; here it is a geometric shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonagon is a plane shape with nine sides, one kind of geometric figure.

clue.text: Minister once said to misbehave

indicators.note: letters that misbehave do not stay in their proper order

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A government minister was once reported to have behaved badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' suggests a politician; the answer is a churchman, and 'once said' is not an old quotation but raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A diocesan is the bishop in charge of a diocese, a senior clergyman, and minister also means a member of the clergy.

clue.text: Live with desire and feel connected

parts.note: to be is to exist or live
to long is to yearn or desire

explanation.surface: Advice to live passionately and feel part of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the two verbs side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To belong somewhere is to be at home in a group or place, fitting in rather than feeling an outsider.

clue.text: Broad-shouldered beast, what only child has that's been raised

indicators.note: in a down clue raising something turns it bottom to top

parts.note: an only child has no sib, short for sibling

explanation.surface: A hefty beast is compared to a solitary, pampered only child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' plays on bringing up a child; in a down entry it tells you to write the letters upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The bison is a large wild ox with a massive humped neck and shoulders, found in North America and Europe.

clue.text: Important clothes we do, right for working?

definitions.text: Important clothes we do, right for working?

parts.note: surface reading: getting our smart outfits on for a big occasion
setter's reading: the style of formal suits worn in offices to project authority and influence

explanation.surface: Someone checks that the smart clothes they put on are right for the office.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the practice: putting on imposing clothes so as to look the part at work.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a 1980s fashion of wearing sharp business suits so as to appear authoritative in the workplace.

clue.text: One had to leave woman alone? Gosh!

indicators.note: what leaves a word is taken out, so 'One had' departs from 'woman alone'

parts.note: a widow is a woman left alone by her husband's death
one had = I had = I'd, the letters removed

explanation.surface: A woman gasps at the thought of someone having to abandon her.
explanation.walkthrough: I'd, the contraction of 'I had', comes out of the middle of WIDOW, leaving WOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of surprise or amazement, used interchangeably.

clue.text: Day extremely full of disagreements, ready for bed

indicators.note: something full of another holds it inside, so the ends of 'Day' hold 'disagreements'
at its extremes a word shows only its first and last letters, here of 'Day'

parts.note: first and last letters of day
rows (rhyming with cows) are quarrels

explanation.surface: After a day of endless arguments, someone is worn out and ready to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: Row here rhymes with cow and means a quarrel, a common British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Drowsy means sleepy and heavy-eyed, the state of someone who needs to turn in for the night.

clue.text: Car reversing in fast bringing medicinal product

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the car goes inside 'fast'

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting

indicators.note: a car reversing goes backwards, so its letters run backwards too

parts.note: the Mini is a small British car

explanation.surface: A car reversing at speed delivers a pharmacy order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' reads as speed, matching the car; it is the religious fast, Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: A liniment is a medicated lotion rubbed into the skin to ease aching muscles or stiff joints.
